expected.quote:
Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. Then $H_i(M,M\setminus K;R)=0$ for $i>n$, and restriction from $H_n(M,M\setminus K;R)$ to all local stalks at points of $K$ is injective. Every continuous section $s$ of the local $R$-homology system on $M$ is realized by a unique class $s_K$ in this relative group.

In particular an $R$-orientation determines a unique $[M]_K$ restricting to its generator at each point of $K$. These classes commute with restriction for compact-set inclusions and split over the finitely many components meeting $K$. No AC is needed.

A continuous map of pairs $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$, meaning $f(A)\subseteq B$,
induces $f_*:H_n(X,A;G)\to H_n(Y,B;G)$ for every $n$. Identity maps and
composites induce identity maps and composites.

The **relative singular homology group** of $(X,A)$ in degree $n$ is
$$H_n(X,A;G):=H_n(C_\bullet(X,A;G))=\ker\bar\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_{n+1}.$$
Equivalently, a relative cycle is an ordinary finite chain $c$ with
$\partial c\in C_{n-1}(A;G)$, modulo adding a chain in $A$ and an ordinary
boundary.

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

Let $M$ be an $n$-manifold with boundary and $x\in M$. For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$,
$$H_k(M,M\setminus\{x\};R)\cong\begin{cases}R,&x\in\operatorname{int}M\text{ and }k=n,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
The boundary subset is independent of charts, and a nonempty manifold's dimension is intrinsic. Homeomorphisms preserve boundary and, for nonempty manifolds, dimension. A manifold is boundaryless exactly when it is locally Euclidean of its specified dimension. Dimension is not intrinsic for the empty space, and the zero coefficient ring cannot detect boundary or dimension; use integral coefficients for these conclusions. No AC is assumed.

expected.claim: If $f^{-1}(y)\cap U=\varnothing$, then $K=\varnothing$ and $H_d(U,U\setminus K)=H_d(U,U)=0$, so $D(f,U,y)=0$. For the identity and $y\in U$, $K=\{y\}$ and the induced map sends the chosen local orientation generator to itself, so $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$.

Under the additivity hypotheses, $K$ is the disjoint union of $K_i=K\cap U_i$. The closed set $Z=U\setminus(U_1\cup U_2)$ has closure in $U$ disjoint from $K$: the compact set $K$ lies in the open set $U_1\cup U_2$. Excision [F3] identifies $H_d(U,U\setminus K)$ with $H_d(U_1\cup U_2,(U_1\cup U_2)\setminus K)$. Since $U_1,U_2$ are disjoint open sets, every singular simplex in their union lies in exactly one of them, so this relative group and its chains split as the direct sum of the two relative groups. The unique orientation class [F1] therefore corresponds to $[U_1]_{K_1}+[U_2]_{K_2}$. The restrictions of $f$ commute with the inclusions of these pairs, so functoriality [F2] maps this sum to the sum of the two target classes. Their integer coefficients consequently satisfy $D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y)$.

For moving-target invariance set $g_t(x)=H_t(x)-y(t)$; translation identifies the target generator with the standard generator at $0$. The zero set $S=\{(t,x):g_t(x)=0\}$ is a closed subset of compact $[0,1]\times\overline U$ and is disjoint from $[0,1]\times\partial U$. Thus its projection $K_*\subset U$ is compact. Every $g_t$ defines a map of the fixed pair $(U,U\setminus K_*)$ into $(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\})$. The singular prism operator for the homotopy satisfies $\partial P+P\partial=(g_1)_\#-(g_0)_\#$; each prism over a simplex in $U\setminus K_*$ avoids $0$, so the chain homotopy descends to relative chains. Hence $(g_0)_*=(g_1)_*$ on $H_d(U,U\setminus K_*)$. Restriction compatibility in [F1] sends $[U]_{K_*}$ to $[U]_{K_t}$ for the actual time-$t$ zero set, so these two induced integers are exactly $D(H_0,U,y(0))$ and $D(H_1,U,y(1))$. They are equal, proving moving-target invariance.

The target group is $\mathbb Z$ by [F4]; the source class is unique by [F1]; and the induced map exists by [F2]. Thus the integer in the Statement is well-defined. Steps 1.1–3.1 establish all asserted properties.

expected.claim: Suppose first that $M>0$ and $w$ has not reached zero by $t_0+2M/\eta$. Integrating $w'\ge\eta/2$ gives $w(t_0+2M/\eta)\ge w(t_0)+M\ge0$, contradicting the assumed strict negativity before the first crossing. Hence the first crossing time $\tau$ exists and satisfies the stated bound. If $M=0$, then $w(t_0)=0$ and $\tau=t_0$.

On $[t_0,\tau]$, $w$ is strictly increasing with $w'\ge\eta/2$, so it is an admissible absolutely continuous time change. Its inverse satisfies $dt/dw\le2/\eta$. If $L>0$, set $p=\epsilon+Lq$. The inequality for $q$ gives $dp/dw\le(2L/\eta)|w|p$, and integration from $w(t_0)$ to $0$ yields $p(\tau)\le\epsilon e^{LM^2/\eta}$. Rearranging gives $q(\tau)\le\epsilon(e^{LM^2/\eta}-1)/L$. If $L=0$, direct integration gives $q(\tau)\le(2\epsilon/\eta)\int_{w(t_0)}^0|s|ds=\epsilon w(t_0)^2/\eta\le\epsilon M^2/\eta$. The same bounds hold with zero right-hand side when $M=0$.

Hence $f_\#\mu(V)=\mu(f^{-1}(V))>0$, so $y\in\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$. Since support is closed, $\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}\subseteq\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$.

expected.quote:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space. A **signed measure** on
$(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function
$$\nu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow \overline{\mathbb R}$$
such that:

1. $\nu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. $\nu$ takes at most one infinite sign: either $\nu(E)\neq-\infty$ for every
   $E\in\mathcal A$, or $\nu(E)\neq+\infty$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$;
3. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in
   $\mathcal A$,
   the series on the right is defined in the extended reals and
   $$\nu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \nu(E_n)$$
   ([[def-extended-reals]]).

The second and third clauses are load-bearing, not stylistic: together they
rule out the undefined form $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$ and require the disjoint
series to exist before countable additivity is asserted.

The next proposition proves the extra fact that if
$\nu(\bigcup_n E_n)$ is finite, then the real series $\sum_n \nu(E_n)$
converges absolutely in the sense of
[[def-absolute-and-conditional-convergence]].

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

expected.claim: The coordinate $w$ is measurable, so $w_+$ and $w_-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. By [F1], $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ are measures, and [F2] gives $\alpha_\mu(\Theta),\beta_\mu(\Theta)\le\int|w|d\mu<\infty$.

For each measurable $B$, $w=w_+-w_-$ and both integrals are finite, so $\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w d\mu=\alpha_\mu(B)-\beta_\mu(B)$. Countable additivity of both finite measures makes their difference countably additive with finite real values, hence a finite signed measure by [F3]. For every countable measurable partition $(B_j)$ of $\Theta$, $\sum_j|h^1(\mu)(B_j)|\le\sum_j(\alpha_\mu(B_j)+\beta_\mu(B_j))=\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta)$; taking the supremum in [F4] proves the stated total-variation bound. For a finite-valued simple $\varphi$, linearity [F5] and the definitions of $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ give $\int\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int w\varphi d\mu$. For general bounded measurable $\varphi$, choose $M$ with $|\varphi|\le M$ and partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$; assigning one endpoint on each measurable inverse image gives a finite-valued simple $\varphi_n$ with $\|\varphi_n-\varphi\|_\infty\le1/n$. The errors in the two $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ integrals are at most $(\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta))/n$, and the error in the $w\varphi$ integral is at most $\int|w|d\mu/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves the identity.

Let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and strongly measurable. Simple approximants to $\varphi$ and to the measurable scalar coordinate $w$ show that $w\varphi(\theta)$ is strongly measurable; moreover $\|w\varphi(\theta)\|\le|w|\|\varphi\|_\infty$, so [F6] makes it Bochner integrable. For each $z\in\mathcal H$, [F7] moves the bounded functional $x\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle$ inside that Bochner integral, and step 2.1 identifies the resulting scalar integral with the pairing in the Definition. Equality of all inner products proves the displayed feature-moment factorization.

$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$

$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

By AC choose couplings $\pi_n$ with $\int(|w-w'|^2+|\theta-\theta'|^2)d\pi_n\to0$. Boundedness and Lipschitz continuity give
$$\|w\varphi(\theta)-w'\varphi(\theta')\|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty|w-w'|+\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)|w'|\,|\theta-\theta'|.$$
By Cauchy–Schwarz, the integral of the right side tends to zero: the first term is bounded by $\|\varphi\|_\infty(\int|w-w'|^2d\pi_n)^{1/2}$, and the second by $\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)(\int|w'|^2d\pi_n)^{1/2}(\int|\theta-\theta'|^2d\pi_n)^{1/2}$, whose first factor stays bounded by W2 convergence.

$$h^2(\mu)(A)=\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}}\mathbf1_A(\rho(u))|u|^2d\mu(u).$$

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

expected.quote:
Assume AC and the full feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_{r_0}$. There is a unique global curve $\mu:[0,\infty)\to\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$ that solves the continuity equation with the negative minimum-norm subgradient velocity of the extended potential $F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega$. For every finite $T$, the curve is concentrated on some $Q_{r(T)}$ and satisfies
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t\int|v_q(u)|^2d\mu_q(u)dq\qquad(0\le s\le t\le T).$$
For any $\mu_0,\nu_0$ concentrated on the same $Q_{r_0}$, their flows obey $\sup_{0\le t\le T}W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{K_TT}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)$ for a finite constant $K_T$ depending only on $T$, $r_0$, and a common upper bound for the initial energies. Consequently, W2-convergent initial laws in a common $Q_{r_0}$ have flows converging uniformly in W2 on every compact time interval.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Fix $r>0$ and a nonempty closed convex constraint $D\subseteq\Omega$. For every continuous moment path $m:[0,T]\to\mathcal H$, the nonautonomous inclusion
$$\dot X(t)\in-\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(X(t))-d\Phi_{X(t)}^*\nabla R(m(t))$$
has a unique forward solution from each $X(0)\in D\cap Q_r$; its characteristic map is jointly continuous in $(t,X(0))$ and locally Lipschitz in the initial point on each $Q_r$. Let $\mu_t$ and $\nu_t$ be two finite-action solutions on $[0,T]$ of the continuity equation with laws concentrated on $D\cap Q_r$ and velocities
$$v_t^\alpha(x)=-\operatorname{argmin}\{|q|:q\in d\Phi_x^*\nabla R(m_{\alpha_t})+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(x)\},\qquad\alpha\in\{\mu,\nu\},$$
where $m_\alpha=\int\Phi\,d\alpha$. The full shifted minimum selection is Borel; it need not be continuous in position. Each finite-action PDE solution with a continuous prescribed feature moment is the pushforward by its unique characteristic map. For starts in $D\cap Q_r$, these characteristics remain in a larger $Q_R$ uniformly on compact time intervals, and their velocity is the negative full shifted minimum almost everywhere. The same construction applies directly to any continuous forcing $a(t)\in\mathcal H$ in place of $\nabla R(m(t))$. Then for all $t\in[0,T]$,
$$W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{(C_r-\lambda_V)t}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0),\qquad C_r=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r.$$
Here $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and $L_r,N_r$ are respectively a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. In particular, the localized measure-valued flow is unique for each initial law. The estimate does not assume that $v_t$ is continuous in position.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, $\gamma(0)$ has law $\mu_0$, and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$, define $\operatorname{spt}\mu=\{x:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$, and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. Define the pushforward by $f_\#\mu(A)=\mu(f^{-1}(A))$ for Borel $A$. Then

$$\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)=\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}.$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let $f:\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. For $y\notin f(\partial U)$, put $K=f^{-1}(\{y\})\cap U$ and define $D(f,U,y)$ by

$$f_*[U]_K=D(f,U,y)[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}\quad\text{in }H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z),$$

where $[U]_K$ is the unique relative orientation class restricting to the standard local generator on $K$, and $[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}$ is the positive local generator. This integer is well-defined. It is nonzero only if $f^{-1}(y)\cap U\ne\varnothing$, and $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$ whenever $y\in U$. If $U_1,U_2\subset U$ are disjoint bounded open sets, $y\notin f(\partial U_i)$ for $i=1,2$, and every point of $f^{-1}(y)\cap U$ lies in $U_1\cup U_2$, then

$$\deg(f,U,y)=\deg(f,U_1,y)+\deg(f,U_2,y).$$

If $H:[0,1]\times\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ and $y:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^d$ are continuous and $y(t)\notin H_t(\partial U)$ for every $t$, then $D(H_0,U,y(0))=D(H_1,U,y(1))$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

expected.claim: Since $R(m_{\mu_t})\le F(\mu_0)$, $\|dR_{m_{\mu_t}}\|$ is bounded on $[0,T]$ by [F1]. Differentiating $\Phi(ru)=r^2\Phi(u)$ gives $d\Phi_{ru}=r\,d\Phi_u$. If $\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$, substitute $y=rz$ into its defining inequality and use $V(rz)=r^2V(z)$; division by $r^2$ shows $r\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(ru)$, and applying the same argument with $1/r$ proves equality of the scaled subdifferentials. The feature-energy bounds on the unit sphere therefore imply $|v_t(u)|\le C|u|$ uniformly on $[0,T]$. Along a characteristic, $r(t)=|X_t(u_0)|$ obeys $|r'(t)|\le Cr(t)$ whenever $r(t)>0$. Grönwall gives $e^{-Ct}|u_0|\le|X_t(u_0)|\le e^{Ct}|u_0|$; the lower bound prevents a nonzero trajectory from reaching zero, while two-homogeneity fixes the zero trajectory.

By [F3], the flow law has a path-space representation concentrated on AC trajectories solving its velocity equation, with initial law $\mu_0$. Each such path solves the nonautonomous characteristic inclusion for the moment path $m_{\mu_t}$; uniqueness in [F2] makes it $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ from its initial point $x$. Therefore $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$. The compact set $K$ has compact image $X_t(K)$; [F4] gives $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=\overline{X_t(K)}=X_t(K)$. Continuity on $[0,T]\times K$ makes $M_K=\sup_{s\le T,u\in K}|X_s(u)|$ finite.

Let $C_\infty$ be the unbounded component of $\mathbb R^d\setminus K$. It is unique because the complement of a sufficiently large ball is connected. Choose $\alpha>\max(r_b,M_K)$ and then $\beta>e^{CT}\alpha$. Set $A=B(0,\beta)\cap C_\infty$. Its boundary lies in $K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$. Moreover $\partial A\cap B(0,r_a)=\varnothing$: if a point of this boundary lay inside the ball, points of $C_\infty$ arbitrarily near it would also lie inside; a path in $C_\infty$ from any such point to outside $B(0,\beta)$ would cross both spheres $r_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and $r_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ without meeting $K$, contradicting separation.

For $y\in\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$, $y\in A$ and $X_s(\partial A)$ avoids $y$ for all $s\le T$: $X_s(K)\subset B(0,M_K)\subset B(0,\alpha)$, while the radial lower bound sends $\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ outside $B(0,\alpha)$. Homotopy invariance [F5] gives $\deg(X_t,A,y)=\deg(\operatorname{id},A,y)=1$. Choose $0<\eta<e^{-CT}r_a$. For every $y\in B(0,\eta)$ and $x\in\partial A$, $|X_s(x)|\ge e^{-Cs}|x|\ge e^{-CT}r_a>\eta$, so the target avoids $X_s(\partial A)$. Since $B(0,r_a)\cap A=\varnothing$, the identity degree there is zero; hence $\deg(X_t,A,y)=0$.

Consider any path from $\eta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and stop it the first time it reaches $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$. Before that time it stays in $\overline{B(0,\alpha)}$, which is disjoint from $X_t(\beta\mathbb S^{d-1})$. If the stopped path avoided $X_t(K)$, then $\partial A\subset K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ would imply that it avoided $X_t(\partial A)$. The degree along that moving target path would be constant by [F5], contradicting its endpoint values $0$ and $1$ from step 4.1. Thus every such path meets $X_t(K)=\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$, proving separation.

expected.quote:
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moment, suppose $\Phi$ and $V$ are continuous and positively two-homogeneous, with $\Phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathcal H$ taking values in a Hilbert space and $V:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}V(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta).$$

If $h^2(\mu_n)$ converges weakly as finite measures on the compact sphere to $\nu$, then the feature integrals converge in Hilbert norm, the regularizer integrals converge, and $F(\mu_n)\to R(\int\Phi d\nu)+\int Vd\nu$. In the partially one-homogeneous model $\Omega=\mathbb R\times\Theta$, $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$ with bounded nonnegative $\widetilde V$, for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the exact feature identity is $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, using the scalar pairing defined in the partial projection, and the penalty inequality is $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu\ge\int\widetilde Vdh^1(\mu)$. Weak convergence of signed $h^1(\mu_n)$ against bounded continuous tests gives weak convergence of feature moments when $\varphi$ is bounded continuous, but does not alone give Hilbert-norm convergence or energy convergence.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of $\mathcal H$ and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative measure on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ such that $\int|w|d\mu(w,\theta)<\infty$. Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Its total variation is finite and satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(\Theta)\le\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta)\le\int|w|d\mu$.

If $\mathcal H$ is a separable real Hilbert space and $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ is bounded and strongly measurable, then for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the feature moment satisfies $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, with the scalar integral defined above. The raw measures $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ record positive and negative parameter weights before cancellation and need not be mutually singular; for example, if $\mu$ assigns mass one to each of $(1,\theta_0)$ and $(-1,\theta_0)$ and zero elsewhere, then $\alpha_\mu=\beta_\mu$ both assign mass one to $\theta_0$ while $h^1(\mu)=0$. Thus the signed projection does not by itself determine a penalty of the form $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$.

u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then there exist positive
measures $
u^+,
u^-:(X,\mathcal A)	o[0,+\infty]$, at least one finite on $X$, such that
$$
u=
u^+-
u^-,$$
and $
u^+\perp 
u^-$.

These measures are unique: if $
u=\mu-\eta$ with positive measures
$\mu\perp\eta$, then $\mu=
u^+$ and $\eta=
u^-$.

The following conditional assertion is choice-free: if a Hahn partition
$X=P\sqcup N$ is supplied, the formulas $
u^+(E)=
u(E\cap P)$ and
$
u^-(E)=-
u(E\cap N)$ construct these unique measures. Comparing
two supplied mutually singular positive decompositions also requires no AC.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite energy, define $F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ on $\Omega$, and extend this potential by $+\infty$ off $\Omega$. Its constrained subdifferential at $u$ is the local Fréchet subdifferential of $F'(\mu)+\iota_\Omega$ defined in the feature-measure-energy convention. A Wasserstein gradient flow from $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ is a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2))$, with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$, for which there is a Borel velocity $v_t(u)$ satisfying the finite-action continuity equation and $v_t(u)$ equals the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega)(u)$ for $dt\,d\mu_t(u)$-almost every $(t,u)$. This definition does not assert that the energy is displacement convex.

Let $M\ge0$, $\eta>0$, $L\ge0$, $\epsilon>0$, and let $w:[t_0,t_0+2M/\eta]\to[-M,0]$ and $\theta:[t_0,t_0+2M/\eta]\to\mathbb R^q$ be absolutely continuous until the first time $w$ reaches zero. Assume $w(t_0)\in[-M,0]$, $\theta(t_0)=\theta_0$, and, almost everywhere before the crossing,

$$w'(t)\ge\eta/2,\qquad q'(t)\le |w(t)|(\epsilon+Lq(t)),\qquad q(t)=|\theta(t)-\theta_0|.$$

Then $w$ reaches zero at some $\tau\le t_0+2M/\eta$. At the first such time,

$$q(\tau)\le \begin{cases}\dfrac{\epsilon}{L}\bigl(e^{LM^2/\eta}-1\bigr),&L>0,\\[4pt]\dfrac{\epsilon M^2}{\eta},&L=0.\end{cases}$$

Thus the crossing remains in $|\theta-\theta_0|<r_0$ whenever the displayed bound is less than $r_0$. The crossing-time bound depends on the initial negative-weight magnitude $M$.

replacement.quote: Let $W:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and $C^1$, and suppose $V(w,\theta)=|w|W(\theta)$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex on $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ for one finite coefficient $\lambda$. Suppose either $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, or $\Theta$ is the closure of a nonempty bounded connected open convex set with $C^1$ boundary and $dW(n)=0$ on that boundary. Then $W\equiv c$ for some $c\ge0$. In the full partial-model hypotheses, the Neumann assumption for $G_f=\langle f,\varphi\rangle+W$ at $f=0$ supplies the latter condition. Consequently, writing $H_+=\langle f,\varphi\rangle+c$ and $H_-=-\langle f,\varphi\rangle+c$, one has $H_-=2c-H_+$ and $\nabla H_-=-\nabla H_+$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $q\ge1$, let $c\ge0$, and let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and continuously differentiable with bounded Lipschitz differential. For $s\in\{-1,1\}$ and $f\in\mathcal H$ put
$$H_{s,f}(\theta)=s\langle f,\varphi(\theta)\rangle+c.$$
Assume one of the following alternatives. In the bounded alternative, $\Theta$ is the closure of a bounded nonempty open convex subset of $\mathbb R^q$ with $C^1$ boundary, and $\partial_nH_{s,f}=0$ on its boundary for every $f$. In the unbounded alternative, $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$ and, for every $f$, $H_{s,f}(r\cdot)$ has a limit $H_{s,f}^\infty$ uniformly in $C^1(\mathbb S^{q-1})$ as $r\to\infty$.

Fix $s,f_0$ and $a_0<0$. Suppose $H:=H_{s,f_0}$ has dense regular values in its range and, in the unbounded alternative, the same holds for $H^\infty:=H_{s,f_0}^\infty$. Values whose level sets are empty count as regular. There exist numbers $a,b$ and $\epsilon>0$ with
$$a_0<a<b<0$$
such that the following two assertions hold on every finite interval $[t_0,t_1]$. Let $f:[t_0,t_1]\to\mathcal H$ be Borel with $\|f(t)-f_0\|\le\epsilon$ for every $t$, and let $\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuous. Every absolutely continuous path $\theta:[t_0,t_1]\to\Theta$ satisfying
$$\dot\theta(t)=-\rho(t)\nabla H_{s,f(t)}(\theta(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t$$
and $H(\theta(t_0))\le a$ satisfies $H(\theta(t))<b$ for all $t$. Every absolutely continuous path satisfying the equation with the opposite sign and $H(\theta(t_1))\le a$ satisfies $H(\theta(t))<b$ throughout the same interval. The constants do not depend on the interval, on $\rho$, or on the order in which the forcing values occur. In particular they apply after reversing time and reversing the forcing path. By decreasing $\epsilon$ if necessary, one also has $H_{s,f(t)}(\theta)\le b/2<0$ whenever $H(\theta)<b$.

Assume AC. Let $\Theta$ be either all of $\mathbb R^q$ or the compact closure of a nonempty bounded convex Euclidean domain and let $\phi:\Theta\to H$ and $W:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded $C^{1,1}$ maps, with $H$ separable Hilbert. Put $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\phi(\theta)$, $V(w,\theta)=|w|W(\theta)$, and assume the feature-energy hypotheses and the prescribed differentiable risk $R\ge0$. Let $\mu_t$ be any flow in the feature-energy Wasserstein definition. Write $m_t=\int w\phi(\theta)d\mu_t$, $f_t=\nabla R(m_t)$, $P_t=\int|w|W(\theta)d\mu_t$, $S(t)=\int w^2d\mu_t$ and $A(t)=\int|v_t|^2d\mu_t$. On every finite interval these quantities have continuous or absolutely continuous representatives as appropriate, and
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t A(q)dq,\qquad S(t)-S(s)=-2\int_s^t(\langle f_q,m_q\rangle+P_q)dq.$$
These identities hold at every finite pair of endpoints. In particular $F(\mu_t)\le E_0:=F(\mu_0)<\infty$ and $\int_0^\infty A(t)dt\le E_0$. If $\sup_{t\ge0}\|m_t\|\le M$, then, with $D=\sup_{R(z)\le E_0}\|\nabla R(z)\|$,
$$0\le S(t)\le S(0)+2(DM+E_0)t.$$
No bounded-support assumption on the initial weights is required.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, $\gamma(0)$ has law $\mu_0$, and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Weak convergence controls the feature term but not the penalty term by [F6]. In the unbounded case choose the outer level regular for both finite and limiting sphere functions, as provided by [F6]. By [F2], the projections eventually remain in that BL neighborhood and the forcing eventually remains within $\rho$ of $f_\nu$. Fix such a time $t_0$ first. Only now use [F5] to choose $M<\infty$ bounding the weights of the entire support at $t_0$. We show that for $t>t_0+M/b$ no negative-weight support point can lie over $K_0$. Take any characteristic with such an endpoint and reverse it on its preceding maximal negative-weight interval. Since $G_{-,t}=2c-H_t$ by [F6], forward on that interval $$w'=2c-H_t\ge b,\qquad\theta'=|w|\nabla H_t.$$ The reversed angular curve, with normalized time change $d\tau/ds=|w|/k(\theta)>0$, follows the favorable negative-gradient field with reversed but still close forcing. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of $\mathcal H$ and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Let $d\ge2$, let $\rho_X$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with finite second moment, and define $s(t)=t|t|$ and $\sigma(t)=\max(t,0)$. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)\in\mathbb R^d$, define the signed-square ReLU feature in $L^2(\rho_X)$ by

$$\Phi(\theta)(x)=\sigma\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}s(\theta_j)x_j+s(\theta_d)\right).$$

The two-copy parameterization uses this feature on one copy of $\mathbb R^d$ and its negative on the other copy; nonnegative measures on the disjoint union represent signed linear combinations of these features. The scalar signed-square map is continuously differentiable with derivative $s'(t)=2|t|$. This definition asserts differentiability of the resulting $L^2$ feature map only when its data law has the additional regularity needed for that conclusion; it does not assert that its differential is locally Lipschitz.

expected.claim:
On a small neighborhood of $(1,1)$ with $w,b>0$, the root $c(w,b)$ is a smooth function of parameters. For an increment $h=(h_1,h_2)$,
$$r_{(w,b)+h}(x)-r_{w,b}(x)=2wh_1x+2bh_2+h_1^2x+h_2^2.$$
The candidate differential is $D\Phi_{(w,b)}h=\mathbf1_{x>c(w,b)}(2wh_1x+2bh_2)$. Outside the interval between $c(w,b)$ and $c((w,b)+h)$, the two preactivations have the same sign; there the ReLU remainder is either zero or $h_1^2x+h_2^2$, whose $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^2)$ by the finite second moment in [F1]. The interval between the two roots has length $O(|h|)$ and lies in a fixed bounded neighborhood of $-1$; on it the pointwise remainder is $O(|h|)$, so its $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^{3/2})$. Thus the full remainder is $o(|h|)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the displayed differential.

At $(1,1)$ the derivative in direction $e_w=(1,0)$ is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-1}$. At $(1,1+\delta)$ it is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-(1+\delta)^2}$. For $0<\delta\le1/4$, their squared $L^2$ distance is
$$4\int_{-(1+\delta)^2}^{-1}x^2p(x)\,dx\ge8p(2)\delta,$$
because the interval lies in $[-2,-1]$, where $x^2\ge1$ and $p(x)\ge p(2)$, and has length $2\delta+\delta^2\ge2\delta$. The operator norm difference of the two differentials is at least their difference on the unit vector $e_w$. Dividing by the parameter distance $\delta$ gives a quotient at least $\sqrt{8p(2)}/\sqrt\delta$, which diverges as $\delta\downarrow0$. Therefore the differential is not locally Lipschitz at $(1,1)$.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, $\gamma(0)$ has law $\mu_0$, and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite energy, define $F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ on $\Omega$, and extend this potential by $+\infty$ off $\Omega$. Its constrained subdifferential at $u$ is the local Fréchet subdifferential of $F'(\mu)+\iota_\Omega$ defined in the feature-measure-energy convention. A Wasserstein gradient flow from $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ is a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2))$, with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$, for which there is a Borel velocity $v_t(u)$ satisfying the finite-action continuity equation and $v_t(u)$ equals the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega)(u)$ for $dt\,d\mu_t(u)$-almost every $(t,u)$. This definition does not assert that the energy is displacement convex.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of $\mathcal H$ and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, $T>0$, and $x:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$ with $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, set
$$Q_P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{\|x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\|_H^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},\qquad C(x)=\sup_P Q_P(x).$$
If $C(x)<\infty$, then there is a strongly measurable $u\in L^2((0,T);H)$ such that $x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ for every $t$, $x$ is norm-differentiable almost everywhere with derivative $u$, and
$$\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt=C(x).$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, let $Y$ be a proper metric space, and let $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be an equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Y)$. If $\{f_k(x):k\in\mathbb N\}$ is bounded for every $x\in X$, then some subsequence converges uniformly to a member of $C(X,Y)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: We first prove a scalar gluing fact, without inferring absolute continuity of a composition with a merely continuous function. Let $I=[u,v]$, let $C\subseteq I$ be closed, let $h:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $Q:I\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous with $h=Q$ on $C$. Suppose that $Q'\le-\kappa$ a.e. on $C$, for some $\kappa>0$, and that $h(t)+\kappa t$ is nonincreasing on every component interval of $I\setminus C$, including its endpoints by continuity. Put $U=h+\kappa t$ and $Z=Q+\kappa t$. If $x<y$ both belong to $C$, the complementary open intervals $(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ of $C$ inside $(x,y)$ have endpoints in $C$. Absolute continuity of $Z$ and countable additivity of its integrable derivative give $Z(y)-Z(x)=\int_{C\cap[x,y]}Z'(t)\,dt+\sum_j\int_{\alpha_j}^{\beta_j}Z'(t)\,dt$. The series is absolutely convergent because the intervals are disjoint and $Z'\in L^1$. Each gap integral equals $Z(\beta_j)-Z(\alpha_j)=U(\beta_j)-U(\alpha_j)\le0$, and the integral over $C$ is nonpositive. Thus $U(y)\le U(x)$. For arbitrary $x<y$, if $[x,y]$ misses $C$ they lie in one gap. Otherwise let $x_*=\min(C\cap[x,y])$ and $y_*=\max(C\cap[x,y])$; monotonicity on the two possible end gaps and the preceding inequality yield $U(y)\le U(y_*)\le U(x_*)\le U(x)$. Hence $h(y)-h(x)\le-\kappa(y-x)$ on all of $I$. This explicitly excludes positive singular variation on the closed contact set; no absolute continuity of $h$ has been assumed or concluded.

The bounded alternative admits a direct trap. Choose a regular value $a\in(a_0,0)$ of $H$, and choose $b\in(a,0)$. If this interval lies outside the range, an empty level set causes no difficulty: on each connected component of $\Theta$, the path cannot cross a missing level by continuity. Otherwise compactness of $\Theta$, the Neumann condition, and regularity give $ eta>0$ with $|
abla H|\ge eta$ on a thin neighborhood of $\{H=a\}$. Since $\|
abla H_f-
abla H\|_\infty\le\|d\varphi\|_\infty\|f-f_0\|$, choose $\epsilon$ so that $\langle
abla H,
abla H_fangle\ge eta^2/2$ on that neighborhood whenever $\|f-f_0\|\le\epsilon$. Along a path in the Statement, $H(	heta)'=-ho\langle
abla H,
abla H_fangle<0$ a.e. while its value is in the thin collar. An outward first crossing of $a$ is therefore impossible: any crossing would contain a subinterval with values in the collar increasing from a lower to a higher value, contrary to the integrated derivative inequality. A start with $H\le a$ consequently remains there. The argument also applies at the intersection with $\partial\Theta$, since the gradients are tangent there by Neumann and the path is constrained to $\Theta$. This proves the first assertion in the bounded alternative.

For the rest of the proof take $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$. Write $r=|	heta|$ and $\omega=	heta/r$ when $r>0$. Choose a smooth radial diffeomorphism $\Psi$ from $\mathbb R^q$ to the open unit ball whose radial coordinate equals $u=1-1/r$ for $r\ge2$, patching it with a smooth strictly increasing radial coordinate near the origin. Its radial coordinate is chosen linear near zero so that $\Psi$ and its inverse are smooth there. Let $M$ be the closed unit ball. Choose a positive smooth radial function $k(	heta)$ with $k=r^2$ for $r\ge2$. The pushforward by $\Psi$ of $-k
abla H_f$ has, in the outer coordinates $(u,\omega)$, the components $(-\partial_rH_f(r\omega),-
abla_{\mathbb S}H_f(r\omega))$. The sphere derivative is zero when $q=1$, where the sphere consists of two points. For fixed $f$, its second component converges uniformly by assumption. Its first converges uniformly to zero: along each ray $r\mapsto H_f(r\omega)$ converges uniformly in $\omega$, and its derivative is uniformly Lipschitz in $r$. If its derivative had magnitude at least $\delta>0$ at arbitrarily large radii, its Lipschitz bound would keep the same sign with magnitude at least $\delta/2$ on a radial interval of a fixed positive length, forcing a fixed nonzero change of $H_f$ there; this contradicts uniform convergence. When that Lipschitz bound is zero, convergence makes the derivative identically zero. Thus the pushed-forward field extends continuously to $M$ with boundary components $(0,-
abla_{\mathbb S}H_f^\infty)$. Denote this continuous Euclidean field on $M$ by $F_f$, and denote by $\widehat H$ the continuous extension of $H\circ\Psi^{-1}$ with boundary value $H^\infty$.

The fields $F_f$ satisfy $\|F_f-F_{f_0}\|_{C^0(M)}\le C\|f-f_0\|$ for a finite $C$. On bounded radial intervals this follows from bounded $d\varphi$ and smoothness of the coordinate change. On the outer region the radial component difference is at most $\|d\varphi\|_\infty\|f-f_0\|$. For the sphere component, consider $T_r:\mathcal H\to C^1(\mathbb S^{q-1})$, $T_rf(\omega)=\langle f,\varphi(r\omega)\rangle$, for $r\ge2$. Each $T_r$ is a bounded linear operator. For every fixed $f$, its assumed convergence as $r\to\infty$ makes its $C^1$ norms bounded at large radii; ordinary $C^1$ regularity on compact radial intervals supplies the remaining bound. Hence [F1] gives $\sup_{r\ge2}\|T_r\|<\infty$. This proves the required sphere bound uniformly in $r$ and, by passing to the pointwise limits, also on the boundary. Smooth changes between these outer coordinates and the Euclidean ball have bounded differentials on the compact outer collar, proving the claimed estimate on $M$. No convergence in operator norm is asserted.

Choose $a\in(a_0,0)$ regular both for $H$ and for $H^\infty$. To justify the simultaneous choice, regular values of $H^\infty$ form an open set, since its critical values form a compact set; density, with empty level sets counted as regular, supplies a nonempty open interval within $(a_0,0)$ consisting of its regular values. Density for $H$ supplies a regular value in that interval. The same reasoning applies if the interval is outside either range. If $\widehat H$ has no values in a neighborhood of $a$, its continuous paths cannot cross that neighborhood, and the desired trap follows immediately. Otherwise choose $d>0$ and $\kappa>0$, with $a_0<a-2d<a+2d<0$, so that the following estimates hold on the band $\mathcal B=\{a-2d\le\widehat H\le a+2d\}$. At interior points the directional derivative of $\widehat H$ along $F_0:=F_{f_0}$ is $-k|
abla H|^2\le-\kappa$; at boundary points the derivative of $H^\infty$ along its boundary field is $-|
abla_{\mathbb S}H^\infty|^2\le-\kappa$. Indeed, near the boundary, uniform $C^1$ sphere convergence and regularity of $a$ for $H^\infty$ bound $|
abla_{\mathbb S}H(r\cdot)|$ below whenever $H(r\omega)$ lies in this band, and $k=r^2$ cancels the Euclidean angular factor $r^{-2}$. The remaining region is compact; regularity of $a$ for $H$ and a smaller band give a positive lower bound there. If the boundary portion of the band is empty, only the compact interior argument is needed.

Every absolutely continuous solution $\gamma:[u,v]\to M$ of $\gamma'=F_0(\gamma)$ whose image lies in $\mathcal B$ obeys $\widehat H(\gamma(v))-\widehat H(\gamma(u))\le-\kappa(v-u)$, even if it touches the compactification boundary on a complicated closed time set. Its speed is bounded by $\|F_0\|_\infty$, so it is Lipschitz. Put $C=\{t:\gamma(t)\in\partial M\}$, which is closed. Choose a $C^1$ function $Q_0$ on $M$ equal to $H^\infty$ on the boundary: on a collar use its radial extension multiplied by a smooth cutoff that vanishes before the collar's inner edge, and extend by zero. This is $C^1$ because $H^\infty$ is $C^1$. The function $Q=Q_0\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous. At a.e. $t\in C$ its derivative equals the boundary directional derivative in step 5.1, since the radial component of $F_0$ is zero there; hence $Q'\le-\kappa$ a.e. on $C$. The continuous function $h=\widehat H\circ\gamma$ agrees with $Q$ on $C$. On any interior gap it is locally absolutely continuous by smooth coordinates and the chain rule, and $h'\le-\kappa$. Integrating on compact subintervals of a gap and taking endpoint limits proves that $h+\kappa t$ is nonincreasing on the whole gap. Apply the scalar gluing argument of step 1.1 to obtain the asserted estimate. In particular this argument does not infer absolute continuity from continuity of $\widehat H$, and does not presume uniqueness for the extended ODE at the boundary.

Fix $\tau_*>0$ so small that every path in $M$ with speed at most $B:=1+\|F_0\|_\infty$ changes the value of $\widehat H$ by strictly less than $d$ on an interval of length at most $\tau_*$. Such a choice follows from uniform continuity of $\widehat H$ on compact $M$, because displacement is at most $B\tau_*$. There exists $e>0$, with $e\le1$, such that every absolutely continuous curve $\gamma:[0,\tau_*]\to M$ staying in $\mathcal B$ and satisfying $|\gamma'-F_0(\gamma)|\le e$ a.e. obeys $\widehat H(\gamma(\tau_*))-\widehat H(\gamma(0))\le-\kappa\tau_*/2$. Otherwise choose curves violating this assertion with errors $e_n\downarrow0$. Their speeds are bounded by $B$, and [F2] gives a uniformly convergent subsequence. Continuity of $F_0$ and the integral equations show that its limit solves $\gamma'=F_0(\gamma)$; the limit stays in the closed band. Step 6.1 gives an endpoint drop at least $\kappa\tau_*$, while uniform convergence and continuity of $\widehat H$ give a drop at most $\kappa\tau_*/2$. This contradiction proves the claim.

Put $b=a+d$. Any absolutely continuous curve satisfying $|\gamma'-F_0(\gamma)|\le e$ a.e. and starting with $\widehat H(\gamma(0))\le a$ cannot reach $\widehat H=b$. For otherwise consider its first time $v$ at level $b$ and its last preceding time $u$ at level $a$. Both exist by continuity, and its values on $[u,v]$ lie in $[a,b]\subset\mathcal B$. The speed bound and the choice of $\tau_*$ force $v-u>\tau_*$. Apply step 7.1 to the final interval $[v-\tau_*,v]$. Its endpoint value must be strictly below its starting value, contradicting that $v$ is the first hit of the upper level $b$. Thus the curve remains strictly below $b$. Choose $\epsilon$ small enough that step 4.1 gives $\|F_f-F_0\|_\infty\le e$ for $\|f-f_0\|\le\epsilon$. The preceding conclusion then holds for every forcing path in that neighborhood, including Borel time-dependent forcing.

For a physical path in the Statement define $\tau(t)=\int_{t_0}^t\rho(v)/k(\theta(v))\,dv$. On each finite interval its derivative is positive and continuous, bounded away from zero, because $\rho$ is positive continuous and the physical path has compact image. Its inverse is consequently continuously differentiable. By change of variable, $\gamma(\tau)=\Psi(\theta(t(\tau)))$ is absolutely continuous and solves $\gamma'=F_{f(t(\tau))}(\gamma)$ a.e. Step 8.1 applies and proves $H(\theta(t))<b$ whenever its initial value is at most $a$. The same argument works on every finite physical interval, regardless of whether normalized time has a finite limit on an infinite horizon. This proves the first assertion in the unbounded alternative.

In either domain alternative, reverse a path satisfying the opposite-sign equation on $[t_0,t_1]$: the path $\widetilde\theta(u)=\theta(t_0+t_1-u)$ satisfies the favorable equation with $\widetilde f(u)=f(t_0+t_1-u)$ and $\widetilde\rho(u)=\rho(t_0+t_1-u)$. These retain the same Borel, continuity, positivity and closeness conditions. The first assertion therefore proves the backward assertion with exactly the same constants. Finally $|H_f-H|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty\|f-f_0\|$, so decrease $\epsilon$ until this bound is at most $-b/2$; then $H<b$ implies $H_f<b/2<0$. The numbers $a,b,\epsilon$ were chosen only from the fixed feature, forcing center and negative level, completing the proof.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of $\mathcal H$ and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. $$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$

derivations.claim: Fix $s>0$ and two points $\theta_0,\theta_1\in\Theta$. Restrict the semiconvex inequality [F1] to the slice $w=s$ and divide it by $s$. Its quadratic error is bounded by $|\lambda|t(1-t)|\theta_1-\theta_0|^2/(2s)$. Letting $s\to\infty$ gives the convexity inequality for $W$, for every $0\le t\le1$.

If $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, restrict $W$ to any line. A nonzero secant slope of a convex function forces its values to grow without bound in one of the two directions: for $a<b<c$, convexity makes the secant slope on $[b,c]$ at least that on $[a,b]$, and the reversed assertion treats a negative slope. Boundedness therefore makes every secant slope zero. Any two points lie on a line, so $W$ is constant.

In the bounded case $W$ attains its maximum at a point $x$ of the compact closure. At an interior maximum $dW_x=0$. At a boundary maximum its tangential differential is zero, because local $C^1$ boundary charts give two-sided differentiable curves in every tangent direction, while the Neumann hypothesis gives zero normal differential. These tangent and normal directions span the ambient space, so again $dW_x=0$. For any $y\in\Theta$, the one-variable convex function $t\mapsto W(x+t(y-x))$ has right derivative $dW_x(y-x)=0$; its secant slope is at least this derivative. Hence $W(y)\ge W(x)$, and maximality gives equality. The final reflected formulas follow by direct differentiation.

Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Put $\lambda_\mu=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu$, so $\lambda_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}|w|d\mu$. Its total variation satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(B)\le\lambda_\mu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume DC. Let $X$ be a Banach space, $Y$ a normed space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of bounded linear operators $X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). If $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|Tx\|<\infty$ for every $x\in X$, then $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|T\|<\infty$, where the norm is [[def-operator-norm]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

derivations.claim: The supremum-norm space $C_b(X)$ is Banach: a uniformly Cauchy sequence converges pointwise, hence uniformly, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous. A signed measure $\sigma$ defines a bounded functional $T_\sigma f=\int f d\sigma$ of norm $|\sigma|(X)$. The upper bound is the variation inequality. For the reverse bound, use [F1] and [F2] to choose disjoint compact subsets of the two Hahn pieces with omitted variation arbitrarily small. The distance formula separating these compacts gives a bounded continuous function equal to $1$ and $-1$ there, with magnitude at most one, whose integral approaches $|\sigma|(X)$. Since $T_{\sigma_n}f$ converges for every $f$, [F3] gives $\sup_n|\sigma_n|(X)<\infty$.

Put $y_n=\sigma_n-\nu$ and suppose their variations are not uniformly tight. Some $\epsilon>0$ then remains outside every compact ball for an arbitrarily late index: each fixed finite set of indices is tight by [F2]. Recursively choose $n_j$ increasing, radii $R_j\to\infty$, and $q_j\in C_c(X)$ with disjoint supports in $\{R_{j-1}<|x|<R_j\}$, $|q_j|\le1$, and $\int q_jdy_{n_j}\ge\epsilon/2$. At stage $j$, choose an index threshold so late that $|\int\sum_{i<j}q_i dy_n|<\epsilon/8$ thereafter, using narrow convergence. Enlarge the exclusion ball to make every earlier-index variation tail smaller than $\epsilon$, and select a later index with tail at least $\epsilon$. Regularity of its positive and negative Hahn pieces and distance cutoffs with compact support in that exterior produce $q_j$ with the required integral. Finally choose $R_j$ larger than its support and with $|y_{n_j}|(X\setminus B_{R_j})<\epsilon/8$. Increasing radii by one leaves gaps between the annuli. The locally finite sum $q=\sum_jq_j$ lies in $C_b(X)$ with $|q|\le1$. Its pairing with $y_{n_j}$ is at least $\epsilon/2-\epsilon/8-\epsilon/8=\epsilon/4$: the earlier terms are small by construction and the entire later sum is bounded by the chosen tail. Batch 51; source item status draft; current Step 1 decision ready. Inspected the full current Definition and proof against consumer hypotheses. Exact supplier excerpt: Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets of $\mathcal H$ and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$

Define h2 by integrating |u|² on angular fibers and h1 by signed w-weight on θ. Distinguish a signed projected measure from a nonnegative lifted representative; never silently treat h1 as positive. Prove the energy/feature-factorization identities and their exact convergence topology, including moment control where needed.
